reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / corneal dystrophy literature
clinicalPearls: The commonest anterior corneal dystrophy, involving abnormal epithelial basement membrane
Slit-lamp examination shows map-like patches, dot-like microcysts and fingerprint lines in the epithelium
Many patients are asymptomatic, but it is a leading cause of recurrent corneal erosion syndrome
Recurrent erosions cause episodes of sharp pain, watering and photophobia, classically on waking
It can transiently blur vision and cause irregular astigmatism
Management targets recurrent erosions with lubrication and, if needed, procedures such as epithelial debridement or stromal micropuncture
reference.pathophysiology: Map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy is characterised by abnormal production and organisation of the epithelial basement membrane, with reduplicated membrane and intraepithelial cysts. Poor adhesion of the corneal epithelium to this faulty basement membrane predisposes to recurrent breakdown, so the epithelium detaches, producing recurrent corneal erosions. The abnormal membrane and microcysts create the characteristic map, dot and fingerprint patterns and can distort the overlying epithelial surface.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent corneal erosion from prior trauma
Epithelial infectious keratitis (during an acute erosion)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination, including retroillumination, for the characteristic patterns
Fluorescein staining to identify epithelial defects during erosions
Corneal topography if irregular astigmatism affects vision
History focused on recurrent erosion episodes
Exclusion of infection during an acute painful episode
redFlags: Signs of infective keratitis complicating an erosion
Significant visual loss from irregular astigmatism or scarring
reference.prognosis: The dystrophy is benign and often asymptomatic; recurrent erosions can be troublesome but are usually controllable, and vision is generally preserved.
pitfalls: Missing an infective keratitis during an acute erosion
Overlooking the dystrophy as the underlying cause of recurrent erosions
Under-treating erosions and allowing recurrent episodes
Attributing visual blur solely to refractive error
management: Lubricate the ocular surface with topical tear substitutes and a hypertonic saline ointment at night to reduce recurrent erosions
Apply a bandage contact lens to promote healing during an acute recurrent erosion
Manage the acute erosion with lubrication, cycloplegia for pain and topical antibiotic prophylaxis, while excluding infection
Offer procedural treatment for refractory erosions such as epithelial debridement, anterior stromal micropuncture or phototherapeutic keratectomy
Reassure asymptomatic patients that the dystrophy is benign with generally preserved vision
Correct irregular astigmatism where it degrades vision
Follow up under ophthalmology and cornea services for recurrent erosion syndrome
